notes.description: A single layer of flattened epithelial cells specialized for rapid diffusion and filtration.
notes.location: Alveoli of lungs, endothelium of blood vessels, Bowman's capsule of kidney.
notes.function: Allows exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products through thin barriers.
notes.features: Very thin cells with flattened nuclei. Cells appear like a mosaic when viewed from the surface.
notes.clinical: Damage to alveolar simple squamous epithelium can impair gas exchange in lung diseases.

notes.description: A single layer of cube-shaped epithelial cells involved in secretion and absorption.
notes.location: Kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, small gland ducts.
notes.features: Round central nuclei with cells approximately equal in height and width.
notes.clinical: Changes in renal tubular epithelium may occur during kidney injury.

notes.description: A specialized epithelium capable of stretching and changing shape.
notes.function: Allows expansion of urinary organs while maintaining a protective barrier.
notes.features: Multiple layers of cells with rounded superficial umbrella cells.
notes.clinical: Abnormal transitional epithelial changes may be associated with urinary tract tumors.

notes.description: Liver tissue organized into hepatic lobules containing hepatocytes and sinusoids.
notes.location: Largest internal organ located in the right upper abdomen.
notes.function: Metabolism, detoxification, bile production, and plasma protein synthesis.
notes.features: Central vein surrounded by plates of hepatocytes with blood sinusoids.
notes.clinical: Chronic injury can lead to fibrosis and cirrhosis.

notes.description: Renal tissue containing nephrons responsible for filtration and urine formation.
notes.location: Retroperitoneal organs on either side of the vertebral column.
notes.function: Blood filtration, electrolyte regulation, and hormone production.
notes.features: Glomeruli, proximal tubules, distal tubules, and collecting ducts.
notes.clinical: Histological changes help identify kidney diseases such as glomerulonephritis.

notes.description: Mineralized connective tissue providing structural support and protection.
notes.function: Support, protection, mineral storage, and blood cell formation.
notes.features: Osteons containing central canals surrounded by concentric lamellae.
notes.clinical: Bone remodeling disorders can affect strength and fracture risk.

notes.description:
A – Lumen

Central space through which blood flows.

B – Tunica Intima

Thin inner layer lined by simple squamous endothelium and supported by subendothelial connective tissue.

C – Internal Elastic Lamina

Prominent wavy elastic membrane separating the tunica intima from the tunica media.

D – Tunica Media

Thick layer composed predominantly of circularly arranged smooth muscle cells.

E – External Elastic Lamina

Elastic membrane separating the tunica media from the tunica adventitia.

F – Tunica Adventitia

Outer connective tissue layer containing collagen fibers, elastic fibers, fibroblasts, nerves, and occasionally small blood vessels.

Description

Muscular arteries are medium-sized distributing arteries that transport blood from elastic arteries to specific organs and tissues. Their thick smooth muscle layer allows regulation of blood flow through vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
notes.location: Examples include radial artery, femoral artery, brachial artery, ulnar artery, coronary arteries, and mesenteric arteries.
notes.function: Distribute blood to organs and tissues. Regulate blood pressure through vasoconstriction and vasodilation. Control regional blood flow according to tissue demands.
notes.features: Thick tunica media composed mainly of smooth muscle. Distinct wavy internal elastic lamina. Round or oval lumen that generally maintains its shape. Tunica media thicker than tunica adventitia. Endothelium lining the lumen. External elastic lamina may be visible.
notes.clinical: Muscular arteries are commonly affected by atherosclerosis, where lipid-rich plaques develop within the tunica intima, narrowing the lumen and reducing blood flow. Persistent hypertension can also lead to thickening of the arterial wall.

notes.description:
Tags

A – Lumen

Central passage through which food and liquids travel.

B – Non-keratinized Stratified Squamous Epithelium

Thick protective lining that resists abrasion during swallowing.

C – Lamina Propria

Loose connective tissue immediately beneath the epithelium.

D – Muscularis Mucosae

Thin layer of longitudinal smooth muscle separating the mucosa from the submucosa.

E – Submucosa

Dense irregular connective tissue containing larger blood vessels, nerves, lymphatics, and esophageal glands.

F – Esophageal Glands

Mucous glands located in the submucosa that secrete mucus.

G – Muscularis Externa

Two muscle layers responsible for peristalsis: inner circular and outer longitudinal.

H – Adventitia or Serosa

Outer connective tissue layer anchoring the esophagus to surrounding structures. Only the short abdominal segment is covered by serosa.

Description

The esophagus is a muscular tube that transports food from the pharynx to the stomach.
notes.location: Extends from the pharynx through the neck and thorax, passes through the diaphragm, and joins the stomach at the gastroesophageal junction.
notes.function: Conducts food and liquids from the pharynx to the stomach. Lubricates the food bolus through mucus secretion. Protects underlying tissues from mechanical abrasion. Propels food by coordinated peristaltic contractions.
notes.features: Thick non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Prominent muscularis mucosae. Submucosal mucous glands. Muscularis externa with inner circular and outer longitudinal layers. Upper third contains skeletal muscle, middle third mixed muscle, lower third smooth muscle. Absence of villi and gastric pits.
notes.clinical: Chronic gastroesophageal reflux may cause Barrett esophagus, in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium.

notes.description:
Tags

A – Lumen

Central air passage through which air flows.

B – Mucosa

Inner lining consisting of respiratory epithelium and underlying connective tissue.

C – Submucosa

Connective tissue layer containing blood vessels, nerves, and seromucous glands.

D – Hyaline Cartilage

C-shaped cartilage ring supporting the tracheal wall.

E – Trachealis Muscle

Smooth muscle located on the posterior aspect of the trachea.

F – Adventitia

Outer connective tissue layer anchoring the trachea.

Description

The trachea is a conducting airway lined by respiratory epithelium and supported by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings.
notes.location: Extends from the larynx at approximately C6 to the carina at approximately T4–T5.
notes.function: Conducts air, filters inhaled particles, moves mucus toward the pharynx, humidifies inspired air, and prevents airway collapse.
notes.features: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. Numerous goblet cells. Thick basement membrane. Seromucous glands. Prominent C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings. Trachealis smooth muscle. No alveoli.
notes.clinical: Smoking damages cilia and impairs mucociliary clearance. Tracheomalacia results from weakening of tracheal support.

notes.description:
A – Lumen

Large central cavity that commonly contains numerous spermatozoa.

B – Pseudostratified Columnar Epithelium

Tall epithelial lining with stereocilia, responsible for sperm maturation and absorption of excess fluid.

The epididymis is a long, highly coiled duct that receives sperm from the testis. Histologically, it is composed of numerous circular or oval duct profiles lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia.
notes.location: Situated along the posterior surface of each testis and continuous with the vas deferens.
notes.function: Maturation of spermatozoa. Storage of sperm prior to ejaculation. Reabsorption of excess testicular fluid. Transport of sperm to the vas deferens.
notes.features: Numerous closely packed coiled ducts. Large lumina often filled with spermatozoa. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia. Smooth muscle surrounding each duct.
notes.clinical: Epididymitis may impair sperm transport and contribute to infertility.

notes.description:
A – Lumen

Central cavity containing numerous spermatozoa.

B – Spermatozoa

Mature sperm cells within the lumen.

C – Pseudostratified Columnar Epithelium

Epithelial lining composed mainly of principal and basal cells.

D – Stereocilia

Long non-motile apical projections.

E – Principal Cells

Tall columnar cells involved in absorption and sperm maturation.

F – Basal Cells

Small cells near the basement membrane.

G – Basement Membrane

Supporting layer beneath the epithelium.

H – Smooth Muscle

Circular smooth muscle surrounding the duct.
notes.location: Located along the posterior border of the testis and continuous with the ductus deferens.
notes.function: Maturation and storage of sperm, reabsorption of luminal fluid, and sperm propulsion.
notes.features: Wide lumen packed with spermatozoa, pseudostratified columnar epithelium, stereocilia, basal cells, and surrounding smooth muscle.
notes.clinical: Obstruction or inflammation of the epididymis can interfere with sperm maturation and transport.

notes.description:
A – Enamel

Highly mineralized outer covering of the crown.

B – Dentin

Thick calcified tissue beneath enamel forming the bulk of the tooth.

C – Pulp Cavity

Central chamber containing connective tissue, blood vessels, nerves, and odontoblasts.

D – Odontoblast Layer

Single layer of cells responsible for dentin formation.

E – Cementum

Calcified layer covering the root.

F – Periodontal Ligament

Dense connective tissue attaching cementum to alveolar bone.

G – Alveolar Bone

Bone surrounding the tooth socket.
notes.location: Embedded within the alveolar sockets of the maxilla and mandible.
notes.function: Mastication, protection of dental pulp, sensory transmission, and support of occlusion.
notes.features: Thick dentin, central pulp cavity, enamel covering the crown, cementum covering the root, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone.
notes.clinical: Dental caries begin with enamel demineralization and may progress into dentin and pulp. Periodontal disease can cause tooth mobility and loss.

notes.description:
A – Urethra

Central passage within the corpus spongiosum.

B – Corpus Spongiosum

Erectile tissue surrounding the urethra.

C – Corpus Cavernosum

Paired erectile bodies responsible for penile rigidity.

D – Trabeculae

Connective tissue and smooth muscle partitions.

E – Cavernous Spaces

Blood-filled vascular spaces.

F – Tunica Albuginea

Dense fibrous capsule surrounding the corpora cavernosa.

G – Deep Artery of the Penis

Artery supplying the erectile tissue.
notes.function: Delivers semen during ejaculation, conducts urine, and achieves erection through vascular engorgement.
notes.features: Two corpora cavernosa, one corpus spongiosum, vascular spaces, tunica albuginea, trabeculae, and deep arteries.
notes.clinical: Erectile dysfunction may result from impaired arterial flow, nerve injury, or erectile tissue disease. Peyronie disease involves fibrosis of the tunica albuginea.

notes.description:
A – Anterior Pituitary (Pars Distalis)

Darkly stained, highly cellular endocrine region.

B – Posterior Pituitary (Pars Nervosa)

Lightly stained region composed mainly of nerve fibers and pituicytes.

C – Pars Intermedia

Thin region between anterior and posterior pituitary.

D – Connective Tissue Capsule

Thin fibrous capsule.

E – Blood Sinusoids

Fenestrated capillaries facilitating hormone release.
notes.location: Situated within the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone.
notes.function: Regulates growth, metabolism, reproduction, lactation, and stress responses. Stores and releases ADH and oxytocin produced by the hypothalamus.
notes.features: Dark anterior pituitary, pale posterior pituitary, pars intermedia, blood sinusoids, and connective tissue capsule.
notes.clinical: Pituitary adenomas may cause hormone excess or compression of the optic chiasm, producing bitemporal hemianopia.

notes.description: test
The adrenal cortex is the outer portion of the adrenal gland. It consists of zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and zona reticularis.
notes.location: Forms approximately 80–90% of the adrenal gland and surrounds the adrenal medulla.
notes.function: Zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone. Zona fasciculata produces cortisol. Zona reticularis produces adrenal androgens. Mnemonic: GFR → Salt, Sugar, Sex.
notes.features: Zona glomerulosa has rounded clusters, zona fasciculata has large pale cells in straight cords, and zona reticularis has smaller darker cells in an irregular network.
notes.clinical: Important disorders include Cushing syndrome, primary hyperaldosteronism, Addison disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and functional adrenocortical tumors.
